```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,

  dev = "ragg_png",

  fig.cap = ""

```

Lately, I've been revisiting my
[earlier](https://dieghernan.github.io/202210_tidyterra-hillshade/)
[posts](https://dieghernan.github.io/202212_tidyterra-hillshade-2/) on
hillshading and the [**tidyterra**
FAQ](https://dieghernan.github.io/tidyterra/articles/faqs.html). I wanted to
understand why two maps made from the same elevation grid could look so
different. How much of that comes from the hillshade, and how much comes from
the way we combine it with the elevation colors?

I started with the [alpha
hack](https://timogrossenbacher.ch/bivariate-maps-with-ggplot2-and-sf/) I used
in my earlier maps and tried it alongside **metR**. That comparison sent me
back to my original map. I'll use the same stretch of southern Spain
throughout so you can see what each change does to the colors and the relief.

## Data and setup

I'm using an elevation grid for the area around Andalusia in southern Spain. I
get the boundary from **mapSpain**, use its bounding box to download the
elevation data with **elevatr** and put the raster in the same coordinate
reference system as the boundary. Every map uses the same grid at zoom level 7,
and every color map uses **tidyterra**'s `etopo1` elevation palette.

The terrain tiles include elevations on land and depths below sea level, so the
map also shows the seabed around the Strait of Gibraltar.

```{r}
#| label: setup-and-elevation-data

library(terra)
library(mapSpain)
library(elevatr)
library(metR)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggblend)

map_family <- "inter-tight"
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_family)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

map_background <- "#faf8f2"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = map_family) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#203b47"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "#203b47"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = map_background, colour = NA),
      legend.spacing.x = unit(0, "pt")
    )
)

# The data
andalusia <- esp_get_ccaa("Andalucia", epsg = 3857)
dem <- get_elev_raster(
  andalusia,
  z = 7,
  clip = "bbox",
  tmp_dir = tools::R_user_dir("elvatr", "cache")
) |>
  rast()

dem <- project(dem, pull_crs(andalusia))
names(dem) <- "elevation"
```

## Hillshade with the alpha hack

I started with the example in the **terra** help. It calculates slope and aspect
from the elevation grid, creates a hillshade with a single light direction and
draws a semitransparent elevation layer on top. I do the same in **ggplot2** and
set the elevation colors to 40% opacity with `alpha = 0.4`.

I set the sun 40° above the horizon, with light coming from the west (270°). I
draw the hillshade in grayscale, then extract the colors with `layer_data()`. I
pass those colors directly to the hillshade layer. That leaves the `fill` scale
free for the elevation palette and its legend.

```{r}
#| label: single-direction-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map of Andalusia. West-facing slopes catch the light,
#|   outlining ridges in the east while the Guadalquivir lowlands stay
#|   mostly smooth.

slope_1 <- terrain(dem, "slope", unit = "radians")
aspect_1 <- terrain(dem, "aspect", unit = "radians")

# Single shadow
hill_1 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = 270)

pal_greys <- hcl.colors(1000, "Grays")

gghill_1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Single-direction hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show

print(gghill_1)

# Get colors

pal_1 <- layer_data(gghill_1) |> dplyr::pull(fill)

plot_brks <- c(-2500, -1500, -500, 0, 1000, 2000, 3500)
plot_labels <- scales::label_comma()(plot_brks)
plot_labels[plot_brks == 0] <- "0 (sea level)"
```

```{r}
#| label: transparent-color-overlay
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with muted greens in the lowlands, ochres in the mountains
#|   and blue offshore. The west-lit ridges show through the pale colors.

map_alpha <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf) +
  geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    alpha = 0.4,
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = plot_labels
  ) +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "Elevation (m)",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.3,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "top",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Transparent color overlay", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_alpha)
```

## Shaded relief with metR

The **tidyterra** FAQ uses `metR::geom_relief()` to draw the hillshade directly
from the elevation grid. I draw the elevation colors on top again. This time I
map `alpha` to elevation, so more of the hillshade shows through in the
mountains.

```{r}
#| label: metr-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   High-contrast grayscale relief map. Alternating dark and light slopes
#|   define the eastern mountains and trace ridges on the seabed south of
#|   the coast.

hill_metr <- ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(aes(z = elevation)) +
  coord_sf(crs = terra::crs(dem), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Hillshade with metR", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(hill_metr)
```

```{r}
#| label: metr-relief-map
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with pale ochre mountains, green lowlands and blue water.
#|   High-contrast shading is most visible in the eastern ranges, where the
#|   elevation colors are more transparent.

map_metr <- ggplot(dem, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_relief(aes(z = elevation)) +
  geom_spatraster(
    data = dem,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    aes(alpha = after_stat(value)),
    maxcell = Inf
  ) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(1, 0.25)) +
  scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
    "etopo1",
    alpha = 0.4,
    breaks = plot_brks,
    labels = plot_labels
  ) +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "Elevation (m)",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.3,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "top",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Elevation-dependent transparency", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_metr)
```

```{r}
#| label: alpha-and-metr-comparison
```

I preferred the **metR** map. Look at the mountains in the east. The ridges
stand out more clearly, and the colors look less washed out. Could I get a
similar result by changing how I combined the hillshade and the elevation
colors?

## Introducing ggblend

[Barney Harris](https://barney.fly.dev/2026/01/27/ggplot2-blending-adventure/)
had noticed the same thing in an earlier version of my Romania map. I'd lowered
the opacity of the elevation layer to let the hillshade through, and the colors
had faded. He showed how to combine the layers with the multiply blend mode in
**ggblend**.

I go back to the hillshade from the first map and switch to
`ggblend::blend("multiply")`. White in the hillshade leaves the elevation colors
as they are. Darker shades darken those colors, so the slopes show through
without lowering the opacity of the elevation layer.

```{r}
#| label: multiply-single-direction-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with deeper greens and blues than the transparent overlay.
#|   Dark slopes add texture to the ochre mountains while the western
#|   lowlands remain mostly smooth.

map_multiply <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_1, fill = pal_1, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = plot_labels
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "Elevation (m)",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.3,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "top",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multiply blend", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_multiply)
```

## Enhancing the hillshading

So far, the light has come from the west. [Dominic
Royé](https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/hillshade-effect/#multidirectional-shadows)
shows what happens when you light the terrain from four directions. He keeps the
sun at the same angle above the horizon and adds the four hillshades together.

I keep the multiply blend and the 40° sun angle. For this map, I average the
hillshades from 225°, 270°, 315° and 360°.

```{r}
#| label: multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map. Highlights pick out ridges running in several
#|   directions across the eastern mountains, with softer shadows on
#|   adjacent slopes.

hill_2 <- shade(slope_1, aspect_1, 40, direction = c(225, 270, 315, 360)) |>
  mean()

gghill_2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = pal_greys, na.value = NA) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multidirectional hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show
print(gghill_2)

# Get colors
pal_2 <- layer_data(gghill_2) |> dplyr::pull(fill)
```

```{r}
#| label: multiply-multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map with textured ochre mountain ridges, deep green lowlands in
#|   the west and blue offshore areas where the seabed texture remains
#|   visible.

map_multi <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_2, fill = pal_2, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = plot_labels
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "Elevation (m)",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.3,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "top",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Multidirectional multiply blend", x = NULL, y = NULL)

print(map_multi)
```

## Jackpot! Stretching the hillshade

An earlier experiment comparing **metR** and **terra** on a Swiss elevation
grid gave me one more thing to try. What if I stretched the hillshade before
blending it with the elevation colors?

I map the 5th percentile of the multidirectional hillshade to 0 and the 95th
to 1. Values in between are rescaled linearly, and anything beyond those
percentiles is clipped to 0 or 1.

```{r}
#| label: stretch-multidirectional-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Grayscale relief map with a pale background and sharper gray shadows
#|   along the eastern mountain ridges and the slopes of the seabed.

# Stretching
q <- as.numeric(quantile(values(hill_2), c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE))

hill_3 <- clamp((hill_2 - q[1]) / diff(q), 0, 1)

gghill_3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, maxcell = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    high = "white",
    mid = "gray80",
    low = "gray20",
    na.value = "transparent"
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Stretched multidirectional hillshade", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Show
print(gghill_3)

# Get colors
pal_3 <- layer_data(gghill_3) |> dplyr::pull(fill)
```

I wanted a brighter result for the final map, closer to the **metR** example.
The stretched values run from 0 to 1, so the ramp goes from `gray80` at the
scale's midpoint of 0 to white at the upper end. I multiply those shades by
the same `etopo1` colors as before.

```{r}
#| label: final-map-with-stretched-hillshade
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Relief map of Andalusia with bright blue bathymetry, green lowlands and
#|   ochre mountains. Fine shadows define the eastern ridges and the seabed
#|   around the Strait of Gibraltar. Labels mark the strait, Sierra Nevada
#|   and the Guadalquivir Valley.

map_final <- ggplot() +
  list(
    geom_spatraster(data = hill_3, fill = pal_3, maxcell = Inf),
    geom_spatraster(data = dem, maxcell = Inf),
    scale_fill_hypso_tint_c(
      "etopo1",
      breaks = plot_brks,
      labels = plot_labels
    )
  ) |>
  blend("multiply") +
  guides(
    alpha = "none",
    fill = guide_legend(
      title = "Elevation (m)",
      direction = "horizontal",
      nrow = 1,
      keywidth = 1.3,
      keyheight = 0.5,
      label.position = "bottom",
      title.position = "top",
      override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Stretched hillshade with multiply", x = NULL, y = NULL)

landmarks <- data.frame(
  name = c("Guadalquivir Valley", "Sierra Nevada", "Strait of Gibraltar"),
  longitude = c(-5.2, -3.3, -5.65),
  latitude = c(37.72, 37.03, 36.1)
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)

print(
  map_final +
    geom_sf_label(
      data = landmarks,
      aes(label = name),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      family = map_family,
      size = 2.7,
      colour = "#203b47",
      fill = map_background,
      linewidth = 0
    )
)
```

Here's the same part of Sierra Nevada at three stages. The last panel shows the
combined effect of the stretch and the lighter gray ramp.

```{r}
#| label: sierra-nevada-detail
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-crop: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Three close-ups of Sierra Nevada compare a west-lit hillshade, a
#|   multidirectional hillshade and a stretched hillshade. The last panel is
#|   brighter, with fine ridges visible across the mountain range.

sierra_nevada <- sf::st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -3.75, ymin = 36.83, xmax = -2.75, ymax = 37.34),
  crs = sf::st_crs(4326)
) |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(terra::crs(dem))) |>
  sf::st_bbox()

sierra_view <- coord_sf(
  xlim = unname(sierra_nevada[c("xmin", "xmax")]),
  ylim = unname(sierra_nevada[c("ymin", "ymax")]),
  expand = FALSE,
  datum = NA
)
detail_theme <- theme(legend.position = "none")

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.92,
  height = 0.92,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 3)
))
print(
  map_multiply + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "West light"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 1)
)
print(
  map_multi + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "Four directions"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 2)
)
print(
  map_final + sierra_view + detail_theme + labs(title = "Stretched hillshade"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 3)
)
grid::popViewport()
```

## Comparing the maps

Each row pairs a hillshade with its color map. The first and third rows share
the same hillshade, so you can compare transparency with multiply blending.

```{r}
#| label: hillshade-comparison-poster
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 19
#| fig-crop: false
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Five rows pair grayscale hillshades with colored elevation maps. The
#|   first and third rows share a hillshade, and multiply blending in the
#|   third row gives deeper colors. The metR row has the strongest grayscale
#|   contrast. The last row brings out fine ridges on a brighter map.

elevation_guide <- ggplotGrob(map_final)
elevation_guide <- elevation_guide$grobs[[
  match("guide-box-bottom", elevation_guide$layout$name)
]]

poster_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_blank(),
  legend.position = "none",
  plot.margin = margin(7, 12, 7, 12)
)
heading_style <- grid::gpar(
  fontfamily = map_family,
  fontface = "bold",
  fontsize = 14,
  col = "#203b47"
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.92,
  height = 0.92,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(
    8,
    3,
    widths = grid::unit(c(0.58, 1, 1), "null"),
    heights = grid::unit(c(0.45, 0.24, rep(1, 5), 0.4), "null")
  )
))

grid::grid.text(
  "Five ways to shade Andalusia",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1:3),
  gp = grid::gpar(
    fontfamily = map_family, fontface = "bold", fontsize = 24, col = "#203b47"
  )
)
grid::grid.text(
  "Hillshade",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 2),
  gp = heading_style
)
grid::grid.text(
  "Elevation colors",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 3),
  gp = heading_style
)

grid::grid.text(
  "Fixed alpha",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_1 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_alpha + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "metR",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(hill_metr + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_metr + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Multiply",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_1 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_multiply + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 5, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Multidirectional",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_2 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_multi + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 6, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::grid.text(
  "Stretched",
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 7, layout.pos.col = 1),
  gp = heading_style
)
print(gghill_3 + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 7, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(map_final + poster_theme, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 7, layout.pos.col = 3))

grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 8, layout.pos.col = 2:3))
grid::grid.draw(elevation_guide)
grid::popViewport(2)
```

Look at the coast in the first and third rows. With multiply, the greens along
the coast and the blues offshore are stronger, even though both maps use the
same hillshade. In the last row, the stretch and lighter gray ramp give the
seabed around the Strait of Gibraltar a brighter look, and I can still pick out
its ridges. That's the version I'd use for this map.
